Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Second seed Andy Roddick is forced to retire with an ankle injury during the first set of his Queen's Club semifinal against fellow-American James Blake, meaning he misses out on a final showdown against British top seed Andy Murray. Andy Roddick feels his ankle injury before retiring from his semifinal against fellow-American James Blake. Roddick, who was bidding for a record fifth title at the London grass-court tournament, injured his right ankle when he slipped at the back of the court in the fourth game of the first set. He eventually called for treatment three games later and resumed only after having his ankle and foot heavily bandaged. However, Roddick was clearly still in some discomfort as he served in the next game and decided to take the safety-first option with Wimbledon starting in just nine days. "I'm going to do everything I can to play at Wimbledon," Roddick told Press Association Sport. "We're scheduled to get it looked at again on Monday and do some scans on it, then we'll see where we're at. "Initial tests have shown the stability and strength is OK. We're looking at days, not weeks. My trainer and doctors don't think anything is torn." Blake, beaten in the 2006 Queen's final by Lleyton Hewitt, admitted he did not take much pleasure from this victory. Speaking after the match, Blake said: "It was unfortunate but Andy is such a great player and he doesn't want to endanger the injury anymore. He normally moves so well and you could tell this wasn't the same Andy Roddick." Meanwhile, Murray swept into his first-ever Queen's final with a ruthless 6-2 6-4 win over unseeded Spaniard Juan Carlos Ferrero. Murray is bidding to become the first Briton to win the pre-Wimbledon warm-up event since Bunny Austin in 1938. The world number three has not dropped a set in four matches and, in reaching his fifth ATP Tour final this year, he also becomes the first British finalist here since Tim Henman in 2002. "I felt it was a good match. I started well but the second set was very close," Murray said in a courtside interview after the match. "I'm obviously happy to win in two sets. I was very happy with the way I played all round. "I didn't have the easiest draw so it's been a good week all around and hopefully I can finish it off on Sunday," added the Scot. In the other men's grass-court tournament being played, second seed Novak Djokovic is through to the final in Halle after a 7-6 6-4 victory over Belgian Olivier Rochus. The Serb will now face unseeded German Tommy Haas, who defeated compatriot Philipp Kohlschreiber 2-6 7-6 7-6 in an epic encounter. Meanwhile, in women's action, Maria Sharapova crashed out in the semifinals of the Birmingham grass-court event, beaten in straight sets by China's Li Na. Russian Sharapova had been bidding for a third victory in the tournament, after winning in both 2004 and 2005, but went out 6-4 6-4 in a match lasting 90 minutes. Fourth seed Li, the highest-ranked player left in the competition, will face Magdalena Rybarikova in the final, after the 13th-seeded Slovakian beat Indian  Sania Mirza 3-6 6-0 6-3.

# Roddick’s Queen’s reign ends with ankle injury

**LONDON, June 17, 2006** — Andy Roddick’s three-year reign at Queen’s Club ended painfully when the American was forced to retire from his semifinal against compatriot James Blake after injuring his left ankle.

The score was level at **4-4 in the opening set** when Roddick stopped, sending Blake into the final of the Stella Artois Championships. Blake was due to face four-time Queen’s champion Lleyton Hewitt, who defeated Britain’s Tim Henman **6-3, 3-6, 6-2** in the other semifinal.

Roddick, the champion at Queen’s in **2003, 2004 and 2005**, hurt himself while changing direction during a rally. He received treatment on court but quickly concluded that he could not continue.

“I heard it crack,” Roddick said. “I’ve sprained ankles before, so I knew what had happened. I tried to walk it off and see if it would loosen up, but it wasn’t getting any better.”

With Wimbledon only days away, the immediate concern was whether the injury would prevent Roddick from competing at the All England Club. The American said it was too early to assess the full extent of the damage.

“I don’t know how bad it is yet,” he said. “Obviously the timing isn’t ideal. We’ll get it looked at and hope for the best.”

Roddick had built one of the tournament’s strongest modern records, winning three consecutive titles and arriving at the semifinal with an **18-match Queen’s Club winning streak**. His powerful serve and aggressive first-strike tennis had made the fast London lawns particularly productive territory.

Blake expressed little satisfaction at reaching the final in such circumstances, particularly against a close friend and Davis Cup teammate.

“It’s unfortunate,” Blake said. “You never want to win a match that way, especially against a friend. Andy has had so much success here, and I know how important this tournament and Wimbledon are to him. I just hope he’s all right.”

## Hewitt ends Henman’s run

Hewitt, the Queen’s champion from **2000 through 2002**, recovered after dropping the second set to Henman. The Australian broke decisively in the final set and used his speed and return of serve to neutralize the Briton’s net attacks.

Henman had raised home hopes by taking the middle set, but Hewitt’s consistency prevailed in the decider.

The result gave Hewitt an opportunity to win a fourth Queen’s title and placed two of the game’s best returners—Hewitt and Blake—opposite each other in the final.

## Federer advances in Halle

At the **Gerry Weber Open in Halle**, world No. 1 Roger Federer kept his grass-court winning run alive by defeating Germany’s Tommy Haas **6-4, 6-7(4), 6-3**.

Federer was tested after Haas took the second-set tiebreak, but the Swiss regained control with an early break in the deciding set. Federer, the reigning Wimbledon champion and a three-time defending Halle winner, advanced to the final against Tomas Berdych.

Berdych reached the championship match with a **6-3, 6-2** victory over Belgium’s Kristof Vliegen. The Czech’s flat ground strokes and strong serving proved too much for Vliegen on the German grass.

## Sharapova beaten in Birmingham

There was also a notable upset at the women’s **DFS Classic in Birmingham**, where American Jamea Jackson defeated top seed and defending champion Maria Sharapova **6-4, 6-4** in the semifinals.

Jackson’s pace and athleticism repeatedly troubled Sharapova, who had won the Birmingham title in both 2004 and 2005. The defeat interrupted Sharapova’s preparations for Wimbledon, where she had been champion in 2004.

Jackson advanced to the final against Russia’s Vera Zvonareva, who beat American qualifier Meilen Tu **6-3, 6-2** in the other semifinal.

The day’s results left the leading grass-court tournaments with sharply contrasting stories: Federer remained in command in Halle, Sharapova suffered a surprise defeat in Birmingham, and at Queen’s, Roddick’s pursuit of a fourth consecutive title was ended not by an opponent but by an untimely injury.

Fifth seed **Tommy Paul** beat fellow American **Sebastian Korda 6-4, 7-6(2)** to reach the final. Paul controlled the second-set tiebreak and said he was pleased to survive “one of the toughest matches” of his week. Her final opponent is unseeded Australian **Ajla Tomljanovic**, who beat fourth seed **Anastasia Potapova 7-6(5), 6-4**. Tomljanovic described the achievement as especially emotional after her long injury absence and said she was proud to be back in a final.
